title: Firing Patterns
intro: Inject the same step of current into different neurons and they answer differently: some fire a steady train that slows down, some fire bursts, some fire fast and never slow, some only fire a burst when the current is switched off. These electrophysiological classes (e-types) are one of the oldest ways of telling cell types apart, and each comes from a specific mix of ion channels that a model has to capture.

blocks.text: Connors and Gutnick (1990) sorted neocortical neurons recorded in slices into three main classes: regular spiking, intrinsically bursting and fast spiking. Gray and McCormick (1996) added chattering cells in cat visual cortex, and later work separated low-threshold spiking interneurons. Thalamic and some other cells add rebound bursting and resonance. The list below names each class, the cells that show it and the channels behind it.

items: Regular spiking (RS): a train whose interspike intervals lengthen during a step (spike-frequency adaptation). Most pyramidal and spiny stellate cells. Mechanism: slow potassium currents that build up with each spike, mainly the M-current (Kv7/KCNQ) and calcium-activated potassium currents (SK, and the slow AHP current).

Intrinsically bursting (IB): an initial burst of two to five spikes riding on a depolarising wave, then single spikes. Many thick-tufted layer 5 pyramidal cells and CA3 pyramidal cells. Mechanism: a persistent sodium or calcium current that outlasts each spike and produces a depolarising after-potential, often helped by dendritic calcium spikes.

Chattering or fast rhythmic bursting (CH/FRB): repeated high-frequency bursts at 20 to 80 Hz. Some superficial pyramidal cells in cat visual cortex and some layer 5 cells. Mechanism: a fast depolarising after-potential that resets quickly, so bursts repeat.

Fast spiking (FS): narrow spikes (around 0.3 ms at half height), high rates (up to several hundred Hz) and almost no adaptation. PV basket and chandelier cells. Mechanism: Kv3 potassium channels that activate only at high voltage and close fast, so the cell repolarises quickly without accumulating slow inhibition.

Low-threshold spiking (LTS): fires at low current, adapts, and can fire a rebound burst after hyperpolarisation. Many SST (Martinotti) interneurons. Mechanism: a T-type calcium current that de-inactivates when the cell is hyperpolarised.

Thalamocortical (TC): two modes. When depolarised, tonic single spikes that encode input linearly; when released from hyperpolarisation, a low-threshold calcium spike crowned by a burst. Thalamic relay cells. Mechanism: T-type calcium (Cav3) plus the h-current.

Resonator (RZ): subthreshold oscillations and a preference for inputs at a particular frequency, typically theta (4 to 12 Hz). Entorhinal stellate cells and some interneurons. Mechanism: the h-current and persistent sodium current together.

Irregular, stuttering and delayed spiking: further interneuron e-types catalogued by the Petilla group. Delayed onset is typical of striatal medium spiny neurons and some neurogliaform cells (slowly inactivating A-type potassium current).

blocks.text: Try it: one equation, many cell types

Izhikevich (2003) showed that a two-variable model, v' = 0.04v² + 5v + 140 − u + I and u' = a(bv − u), with a reset v ← c, u ← u + d after each spike, reproduces all of these classes by changing only a, b, c and d. Pick a class below and compare the spike trains. Regular spiking slows as u builds up; intrinsically bursting starts with a burst (higher reset c, so the cell restarts close to threshold); chattering repeats bursts; fast spiking keeps a high constant rate (fast recovery a = 0.1, small d); the thalamocortical preset barely adapts (d = 0.05).

widget.title: Firing classes of the Izhikevich neuron

blocks.text: The widget only shows responses to a positive step. Rebound bursting, the signature of thalamocortical and LTS cells, needs a hyperpolarising step followed by release; see Thalamic Neurons (#/neuroscience/cell-types/thalamic).

blocks.source:
Common e-type features (current-step protocol)

rheobase           smallest step current that evokes a spike
f-I slope          extra Hz per extra pA above rheobase
adaptation index   mean over n of (ISI_n+1 - ISI_n) / (ISI_n+1 + ISI_n)
                   ~0 for FS, clearly > 0 for RS
burst index        fraction of spikes with ISI < 10 ms at step onset
AP half-width      ~0.3 ms FS interneuron, ~1 ms pyramidal cell
AHP depth          undershoot after the spike, mV below threshold
sag ratio          (peak - steady) / peak of a hyperpolarising step;
                   large when the h-current is strong
rebound spikes     spikes after release from hyperpolarisation

blocks.text: What this means for your SNN

items: Excitatory populations: regular spiking with adaptation is the safe default. Adaptation lowers rates under sustained input and makes cells respond to change, which matters for prediction and novelty signals.
Inhibitory populations: fast spiking for PV-like cells so inhibition can follow excitation within a few milliseconds; low-threshold spiking for SST-like cells.

Bursts are information: a burst from a layer 5 cell can signal that bottom-up and top-down input coincided (see Layer 5 Pyramidal Cells, #/neuroscience/cell-types/cortical-excitatory/l5-pyramidal). A model whose excitatory cells can only fire single spikes loses that channel.

Plain LIF has no adaptation and no bursting. Adding one adaptation variable (AdEx, or LIF plus an adaptation current) recovers RS, and the AdEx b and reset parameters can also give bursting (Naud et al. 2008).
